Like in previous PRs, I'm removing the "order" debug fields.
They served to return the methods ordered by registration order instead of randomly, but only in DEBUG.

Since we don't want unexpected discrepancies between DEBUG and RELEASE, I simply removed this behavior. There is little benefit to it. The API hasher sorts before hashing.

I'm not totally sure about the reason for this implementation, cc @dsnopek 

The way it works currently seems to be leaking the GDType, along with a bunch of other things from `ClassInfo`?

Calling `free_method_binds()` is a no-op in this case; it does the exact same as what the code currently does, but this really smells fishy.

Notably, the order in the new version is different than in the previous implementation: It no longer lists subtypes' methods first, and then supertypes' methods.
Since it impossible to effectively act on the order (it is random within the class, and it is impossible to know when one class' methods stop and the supertypes' start), I see no reason to keep this behavior.

Previously, the `p_exclude_from_properties` boolean was only respected in DEBUG, not in RELEASE. In RELEASE, it was silently ignored. It is also ignored for compat methods.

I have no idea what this means and if this has a consequence. Differentiating between DEBUG and RELEASE seems wrong anyway, so I changed it to affect all builds.

Moving this (the `!has_method` check) down here will remove the `method_map` cross check for compat methods.
It would be nice to keep it, and I will probably re-introduce it in a future PR when compat methods are moved to `GDType`.

Nvm, `methods_in_properties` is DEBUG only too, so it needs to be DEBUG protected.
I guess it's just a safeguard we don't want the overhead of in RELEASE maybe...

I understand the functioning of the second if clause being in the `#ifdef #endif` guards, but I really think it would be better to extract it to its own guarded `if (condition) { continue; }` since they are or'd (`||`). The added readability benefit imo outweighs the verbosity "cost" of two extra lines of code.
same here
May be worth leaving a comment about it in the code then.

These two not being able to use `get_gdtype_static().get_method_map(false).get_ptr("get_path")` (since we'd need to include, which would be circular) is a shame.
What's your opinion on extracting `ObjectDB` from `Object` to resolve this issue?

Somehow, I'm getting a worse performance with this PR, *unless* these maps are a regular `HashMap` (then it's slightly better).

If it's useful info, in the past I was randomly testing changing each `HashMap` from `ClassDB` to `AHashMap`, and eventually opened #112129, in which I avoided changing `method_map` as it made performance worse.

Do we have any clues as to why perf on a `StringName`-keyed map would be worse for `AHashMap` vs `HashMap`?

The expense either has to be due to differences in `get` overhead or issues with construction/resizing. I don't know what else it would be here.

Perhaps `AHashMap::_lookup_idx_with_hash` is slower than `HashMap::_lookup_idx_unchecked` for `StringName` keys?

This does look a bit weird. Given that `classes` has value-keys, calling `classes.erase` is going to delete the `ClassInfo`, but `ClassInfo` only has a default dtor meaning it doesn't really do any cleanup for its various pointer members (nor can I even tell what the expected ownership model is from just looking at it).

The call site is in `GDExtension::_unregister_extension_class`
```c++
#ifdef TOOLS_ENABLED
	ClassDB::unregister_extension_class(class_name, !ext->is_reloading);
#else
	ClassDB::unregister_extension_class(class_name);
#endif
```

So it wants to keep the method binds around during a reload for... undocumented reasons.

It _appears_ to be a way to cross-communicate with `GDExtension::_register_extension_class_method` to avoid recreating the `GDExtensionMethodBind` objects, instead updating the existing ones with the reloaded extension data. It only does this if `TOOLS_ENABLED` though (I suppose reloads are not legal otherwise).

The context from the [original PR](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/80284) is
```
When methods are gone after the reload, it marks the method binds as "invalid" and if you try to call them an error is printed and it won't be called. However, if something is caching method binds, it should probably check if it's still valid, and if not, stop caching it! If GDScript or anything else in the engine is doing this, we should update it. This could be handled in a follow-up PR - what is in this PR is at least safe.
```

So... Maybe a bandaid over poor behavior of things holding onto `MethodBind*` objects when they ought not to be.
Is there a brief explanation for what "with compatibility" entails?

Our own BunnyMark measurements [highly fluctuate](https://benchmarks.godotengine.org/graph/rendering-bunnymark/). IIRC you've been saying you use another implementation, but your measurements have also highly fluctuated across different PRs, with different results every session.
Besides, I highly, highly doubt that BunnyMark is so bottlenecked by method info lookups that this PR would affect it by 4%, let alone to worsen it.
You ignored my plea to fix your measurement approach last time, so this time I'm just going to close this discussion and ignore the measurement without any further explanation.

It's used for backwards compatibility. When we bind methods in `_compat`, they are meant for GDExtensions that happen to call the old version of the function. Those implementations will call this method with the hash from the API they build against, and then they will receive the compat function binding back instead of the latest one.

This would be incorrect. This is getting the bindings for `Node` and `Resource`. `get_gdtype_static().[...]` would attempt to get it for `Object`, which would fail.
The reason we don't use `Node::get_gdtype_static().[...]` is not because of circular dependency (we could easily include it from the CPP), but because the current consensus is that core types should not include scene types if it can be avoided.
I think that makes little sense, because the dependency is there just as well (just hidden), but it's out of scope to question it here.

I'm worried about the situation where `MethodBind*` are destructed, but `GDType` isn't, because then if `GDType` destructs it will definitely segfault. The alternative is if the `GDType` was leaked, which would be similarly wrong.

I should have been more precise, yeah `Node::` and `Resource::`. 
I'll see about opening a PR after this is merged to split it up and see about adding those includes, hopefully the separation makes the inclusions more "acceptable".

I agree in theory that it would be yet another type crime, but we have enough of those that unless we can prove this behavior does not exist within the codebase, we should not create the "regression".
That or fix the existence of the behavior first.
May be worth discussing in a core meeting, but my gut feeling is a separate PR to fix the behavior (first or after, since it's unexpected either way).

Good catch!

Perhaps it would be good in the future to soft-leak the whole `GDType` object instead of just methods? It should be an acceptable cost, and would allow users everywhere to assume they stay intact forever (as is the case in not hot reloadable builds).

Tried it but had to revert the change because `base_obj` can be null after the call.
The current implementation is somewhat inefficient, but out of scope to improve.

I think I fixed it. At least it's no longer crashing at exit :D

Essentially, I'm doing exactly that now: Whole `GDType` gets soft leaked (which should be acceptable because it's not huge); added to an autorelease pool and gets purged on `ClassDB` cleanup.
`ObjectGDExtension` no longer owns `GDTypes` at all, they're now created, attached and destructed by `ClassDB`.

These were previously used to clean up and destroy old outdated `GDExtension` methods.

In the new version, they are soft-leaked instead, along with their owning `GDType`. This should be safer overall, and nicely conforms to `GDType`'s promise of "immutable after creation".

What does "soft leak" mean in this context (specifically the "soft" part)? Skimming the code briefly, it just seems like they are leaked now? Which isn't necessarily bad - we were cleaning them up when the GDExtension was fully unloaded, which usually only happens when Godot exits anyway, and any leaked memory would go away at that point

It's cleaned up when Godot exits. The `MethodBind` instances are now all owned by `GDType`, and all `GDTypes` that are registered in the `ClassDB` once are kept alive until exit (upon which they are freed, through the two autorelease pools).
